teaching.causalExplanation: The satellite does move. The trick is that the ground under it moves too. Earth turns once a day, so if the satellite goes round once a day, in the same direction, it keeps pace with the spot below it. So the first requirement is a period equal to Earth's rotation period. That's actually twenty-three hours fifty-six minutes, because Earth turns once relative to the stars in that time, but most questions use twenty-four hours. Last time, we saw that choosing the period chooses the radius. Rearrange r cubed over T squared equals big G M over four pi squared, and r cubed equals big G M T squared over four pi squared. With T as twenty-four hours, which is eight point six four times ten to the four seconds, r cubed is about seven point five seven times ten to the twenty-two. Take the cube root, and r is about four point two three times ten to the seven metres from Earth's centre. Subtract Earth's radius, and the altitude is about three point five nine times ten to the seven metres, roughly thirty-six thousand kilometres up, more than five and a half Earth radii. Its speed is two pi r over T, about three point zero eight kilometres per second. That's much slower than the station's seven point seven, just as a higher orbit should be.

Calculations use 24 h = 8.64 × 10⁴ s as HSC questions and the site do; the sidereal radius (4.222 × 10⁷ m) differs by 0.2 % (author note a).

- **Direction and shape.** West to east; a westward 24 h orbit would pass overhead twice a day (relative angular speed doubled; author note b). Circular so the speed stays constant (the site's "east-west drift" reason).

Limits: signal up and down about 0.24 s (site "~240 ms"); low or absent at high latitudes (beyond about 81° latitude the satellite is below the geometric horizon; author note d).
- **Near Earth (site regions list).** LEO a few hundred kilometres: period about 90 minutes in speech, crosses the sky in minutes; close imaging, a crewed station, low-delay internet constellations; needs many satellites and tracking dishes. Revision 2: the table and key note give the class range 200 to 2,000 km with about 90 to 130 min (88 min at 200 km, 127 min at 2,000 km in the model), because one class-wide "about 90 min" is wrong at the top of the range. The Revision 2 visual upgrade is already written into each scene's Visual line (anchor, simulation, colour roles, hand tags, framed answers). This section tops the design up to the checklist used for Year 11 Physics, Biology and Chemistry, and applies root rules R1 to R4 (`../checks/root-acceptance-y11-upgrade-12-nov.md`). scenes.teachingReason: The satellite does move. The trick is that the ground under it moves too. Earth turns once a day, so if the satellite goes round once a day, in the same direction, it keeps pace with the spot below it. So the first requirement is a period equal to Earth's rotation period. scenes.teachingReason: But the right height and period still aren't enough. Gravity pulls towards Earth's centre, so the plane of every orbit passes through Earth's centre. Tilt the orbit, and for half of each day the satellite is north of the equator, and for the other half it's south. From the ground, it would drift up and down the sky. That's called geosynchronous, but not geostationary. The only orbit that stays above one latitude all day is the one in the equator's plane.

scenes.teachingReason: Two more conditions. It must travel west to east, the same way Earth turns, or it would pass overhead twice a day instead of staying put.
